mstts:express-as.prosody: Let’s talk about something that’s actually pretty complicated when you stop and think about it—recognition. Some people seem to get it without even trying. Their names end up in books, their faces are cast in stone, and their stories just keep getting told. But for others, recognition is always a little out of reach. And really, when we look at Ali’s story, it’s all about what it feels like to be noticed—or to go unseen. Picture this: there’s a moment described in the book where someone’s standing in a museum, staring at a glass case full of birds that Wallace collected. The labels are perfect, every bird is carefully arranged. But there’s no mention of the hands that actually gathered them, or the sharp eyes that first caught those flashes of color up in the trees. The visitor feels it right away—something’s missing. The story just isn’t complete. If you’ve always been recognized, you might not even notice what it means to be seen. But for people like Ali, who did all the hard work but never got the credit, that absence is real. It’s not just about having your name somewhere. It’s about dignity—it’s about being known and valued for what you’ve done and who you are. The book spends a lot of time on this idea: recognition isn’t just handed out. It’s shaped by power—by who gets to tell the story, and whose voices actually get heard. For Ali, not being recognized wasn’t just a personal insult. It was part of a bigger pattern—a system that decided whose lives were worth remembering, and whose could quietly fade away. But you know what? Sometimes, there were these small moments of recognition. Out in the field, Wallace would sometimes praise Ali’s skill, trust his judgment, and lean on his companionship. These moments didn’t always make it into the record books, but they mattered. They were little flashes of being seen—of someone acknowledging the person behind all the hard work. In the end, searching for Ali is really about searching for recognition—not just for him, but for everyone whose efforts have been quietly overlooked. It’s a powerful reminder: to be seen is to be affirmed, to be given your place in the story of the world.
